These examples show step by step how to solve and estimate nonlinear macroeconomic models
with neural networks. They accompany the paper [*Estimating Nonlinear Heterogeneous Agent Models
with Neural Networks*](https://www.hannokase.com/research/deep-learning-zlb/KMR_NeuralNetwork_Hank.pdf).

The examples start with a linearized New Keynesian model and ten extensions of it, and then
move to heterogeneous agent models, the Krusell–Smith model with one and two assets and a
heterogeneous agent New Keynesian (HANK) model.
[How the examples are organized](#how-the-examples-are-organized) describes them in turn.

## The method at a glance

The method has two parts.

1. An **extended neural network** solves the model for many parameter values at once.
2. A **neural network particle filter** then approximates the likelihood, so that
   estimation does not need to run a particle filter at every parameter value.

### Solving the extended model

**1. Map the model to the general form.** Write the model in terms of its state variables
$\mathbb S_t$, shocks $\nu_t$, and the policy functions $\psi_t$ that the network will learn.
Split the parameters into those to estimate, $\tilde\Theta$, and those to calibrate,
$\bar\Theta$. In a heterogeneous agent model the continuum of households becomes a finite but
large number $L$ of households, and the state contains every household's state together with
the aggregate states.

**2. Parametrize the policies with an extended network.** A deep neural network approximates
the policy functions,

$$\psi_t=\psi_{NN}\bigl(\mathbb S_t,\tilde\Theta\mid\bar\Theta\bigr).$$

The parameters to estimate enter as inputs, like states. We call them pseudo-state variables.
The network is trained once and can then be evaluated at any parameter value without solving
the model again. Heterogeneous agent models use one network for individual policies and one
for aggregate policies.

**3. Turn the equilibrium conditions into a loss.** Each equilibrium condition becomes a
residual $F_j$ that is zero at the solution. Conditional expectations are averages over Monte
Carlo draws of next-period shocks. Occasionally binding constraints, such as a borrowing limit,
become a Fischer–Burmeister condition. The loss is a weighted mean of the squared residuals
over a batch of simulated economies.

**4. Train by simulating the economy.** Training uses stochastic gradient methods. Each economy
in the batch has its own parameter draw. After a few gradient updates, the economies are
simulated forward with the current network, and from time to time new parameters are drawn.
The network therefore trains on states and parameter values where the model economy actually
spends its time.

### The neural network particle filter

The likelihood of a nonlinear model is evaluated with a particle filter. With the extended
network, a single evaluation of the solution is fast. But the particle filter evaluates it for
thousands of particles in every one of hundreds of periods, and estimation needs the likelihood
at many parameter values. The particle filter therefore becomes the bottleneck.

**1. Generate a likelihood dataset.** Run the particle filter once at many parameter draws,
spread over the parameter space with a Sobol sequence. This gives a dataset of parameter
vectors and their log likelihoods.

**2. Train the likelihood network.** A second neural network learns the map from parameters
to log likelihood. Part of the draws is held out for validation, to check that the network
also fits parameter values it has not seen.

**3. Use it in estimation.** The trained network returns the likelihood almost instantly, so it
can replace the particle filter inside Bayesian estimation. The examples here compare the
likelihood network with the particle filter. The paper and its replication package carry out
the estimation.

## How the examples are organized

The use of different models serves two purposes. First, several models give a clear,
incremental learning path for researchers interested in solving and estimating nonlinear
heterogeneous agent models with neural networks. The New Keynesian model is substantially
faster to solve and does not require access to a GPU, so it is very well suited to introduce
the key features of our solution approach and the neural network setup. The inclusion of
heterogeneity requires some adaptations to the code, which makes the heterogeneous agent
examples essential. Second, the code for these models is a starting point for other
researchers who wish to work with neural networks. For this reason, we focus on these seminal
models.

The examples are organized in two tiers. The second moves from a representative household
to a distribution of households.

### 1. The New Keynesian model

The [baseline](rank/index.qmd) is the linearized three-equation New Keynesian model, the
first proof of concept in the paper. It shows the full workflow, from solving the model with
the extended network to approximating its likelihood. Because the model has an analytical
solution, we can check the network's policies against it. It runs on a laptop CPU.

Ten extensions then change one element of the baseline at a time. Each starts from the
previous one, so together they build up a richer model step by step.

+===============================+====================================================+========================+

+-------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+                        +

+-------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+                        +
| [4](rank/extension-04.qmd)    | Shocks as exogenous state variables                |                        |
+-------------------------------+----------------------------------------------------+                        +

### 2. Heterogeneous agent models

The heterogeneous agent models apply the same recipe to a distribution of households with
idiosyncratic income risk and a borrowing limit. Their networks take the whole distribution as
input, and each solution is checked against the sequence-space Jacobian (SSJ) method. The
[Krusell–Smith model with one asset](ks/one-asset.qmd) introduces the two-stage solution, first
the deterministic steady state and then the economy with aggregate risk. The
[two-asset version](ks/two-asset.qmd) adds a government bond, so households choose a portfolio.
The [one-asset HANK model](hankmp/index.qmd) adds sticky prices, labor supply, and a
monetary-policy shock whose persistence is a pseudo-state variable.

### Structure of each example

Every page follows the same order. It states the model, maps it to the general form, walks
through the code that changes, and ends with the results. Each code block names the script it
comes from.

Every example is a Python script, and the `notebooks` folder next to it holds a Jupyter
notebook with the same code. Each New Keynesian script contains the complete model, so every
extension runs on its own.

To see exactly what an extension changes, compare its script with the previous one. In VS
Code, select the two scripts in the Explorer, right-click, and choose *Compare Selected*, or
run `code --diff rank_extension_02.py rank_extension_03.py` from `examples/rank`. The
differences are a few dozen lines each. Only the policy plots come from
`rank_plots.py` in the same folder. The heterogeneous agent examples keep their model,
analysis, and plotting code in separate files, as in the replication package.

Each example ships with its trained networks and saved results, which load by default. The
flags at the top of each script retrain any stage. The first cell of each notebook moves to the
example folder, where the helper modules and outputs are.

To run the examples, first [set up Python](setup.qmd).
